# Day 6 — Consolidation {#sec-day6-consolidation}

**20 minutes · plenary**

## Say it in one sentence

An explanation is a statement about the model. It is not a statement about the
patient, and it is not evidence about the disease.

Everything today was a demonstration of that sentence. A column of random
numbers was ranked fifth of nine by the forest's own importance measure, and
the model was no worse without it. A force plot gave a faithful, exact account
of a predicted probability of 0.71 for a woman who did not have diabetes. A
forest fitted to shuffled labels, scoring an AUC of 0.47, produced a SHAP
summary as orderly as the real one. A partial dependence curve for insulin ran
smoothly across values that, for half the patients, were never measured.

None of those figures was wrong. Each was a correct answer to a question about
a fitted function, read as though it were an answer to a question about people.

## Self-assessment

- [ ] I can say what impurity importance measures, and why a pure-noise column
      scores highly on it.
- [ ] I can say what permutation importance measures, and why it needs held-out
      rows.
- [ ] I can state the SHAP additivity identity and check it in code.
- [ ] I can read a beeswarm plot and a force plot aloud without making a claim
      about the patient.
- [ ] I can name the assumption a partial dependence profile makes, and a
      variable in `data/diabetes.csv` for which it fails.
- [ ] I can build a DALEX explainer around a tidymodels workflow and check that
      it has the outcome the right way round.

## Questions

1. Two importance measures rank the same model's variables differently. Your
   collaborator asks which is correct. Answer in two sentences.
2. You are shown a beeswarm plot for a model you did not fit. Name the two
   things you must know before you read anything off it.
3. A patient's force plot shows glucose contributing +0.31. She asks whether
   lowering her glucose would lower her risk. What do you say?
4. `noise` scored 37% of glucose under impurity importance, 12% under mean
   absolute SHAP, and about zero under permutation importance. Put those three
   numbers in order of how much they tell you about the *data*, and justify the
   order.
5. You have a model with an AUC of 0.47 and a beautiful SHAP summary. What is
   the correct next action, and what would be the wrong one?

::: {.content-visible when-profile="instructor"}
::: {.instructor}
**Answers.** (1) Neither is incorrect; they measure different things — one
counts how the forest was built, the other measures what the predictions lose
without the variable — so the question to return is which of those the
collaborator meant to ask. (2) The held-out score against a baseline, and the
scale of the x-axis. (3) That the plot describes how the model computed its
output, not what would happen to her; the question she is asking is causal and
needs a different study design, and the honest answer is that nothing shown
today can address it. (4) Permutation tells you most about the data because it
is measured on rows the model never saw and is scored by predictive loss; SHAP
next, because it is faithful to a model that may or may not be any good;
impurity least, because it is computed entirely from the training fit and never
looks at an outcome it has not already used. The sharper version: all three
tell you about the model, and they differ only in how much the model had to
earn the number. (5) Correct: discard the model, or go back to the data. Wrong:
publish the SHAP plot. There is a weaker wrong answer worth drawing out — "tune
the hyperparameters until the AUC improves" — which, repeated on the same test
set, manufactures the score rather than the model.

**Rubric.** A student who has the day has stopped saying "the model found that
glucose is important" and started saying "the model used glucose most". If
question 3 produces anything other than a refusal to answer causally, spend the
remaining time there rather than on the others — it is the misreading that
survives the module and reaches a clinic.

**One thing to show if there is time.** Re-run the shuffled-label cell from
@sec-shap with a different seed in front of the room. The AUC moves around 0.5
and the SHAP plot stays confident and keeps changing its mind about which
variable leads. That instability is the only visible symptom, and it is only
visible because you ran it twice.
:::
:::

## What carries out of the module

Three loose ends were left deliberately, and all three are where this material
goes next.

1. **Explanation is not causation, and today had no way to close that gap.**
   Everything on Day 6 describes a fitted function. The question clinicians
   actually ask — what happens if we intervene — needs a causal framework, and
   a SHAP value is not one.
2. **The model was never tested outside its own extract.** Every figure today
   rests on 231 held-out rows from the same file as the 537 it was fitted on.
   @sec-shift showed what happens when that assumption breaks; nothing since
   then has re-examined it.
3. **The explanations themselves were never validated.** We checked the
   arithmetic of SHAP and the control behaviour of the importance measures, but
   we never asked whether an explanation is stable across resamples of the
   training data. Refit the forest on a different split and the ranking below
   glucose rearranges itself. An explanation with no uncertainty attached is an
   estimate reported without a standard error.

@sec-roadmap has the reading, and the module leaves you with the only durable
habit on offer: before you explain a model, show that it is worth explaining.
